47	\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
48	\seclabel{static-arg-inference}
49	
50	The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
51	steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
52	instantiated second.
53	
54	\emph{Choice.}
55	The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
56	A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
57	coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
58	applicable to the call.
59	Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
60	with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
61	its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
62	So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
63	declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.
64	
65	\emph{Instantiation.}
66	The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
67	the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
68	\begin{itemize}
69	\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
70	declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
71	\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
72	the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
73	type of the instance.
74	\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
75	declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
76	expected type as well.
77	\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
78	parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
79	takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
80	which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
81	(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
82	substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
83	the type parameter permit.
84	For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
85	converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
86	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
87	\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
88	(\secref{basic-integers}).
89	Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
90	(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
91	the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has
92	none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type (below), where the call
93	has one, requires of the declared return type, provided the types of those
94	arguments are subtypes of it; none of those arguments is converted.
95	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 gave such
96	a type parameter the union of the types of those arguments; on 29~September 2026
97	the revival took the rule by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
98	2019 instantiates a type parameter, which gives the bound.}
99	\item A type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes as
100	above, such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole
101	type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound,
102	\TYP{Any} if it has none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type
103	(below), where the call has one, requires of the declared return type.
104	Inference never instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, which
105	programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}).
106	So, for the declaration
107	\EXP{\VAR{stop}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(s\COLON\TYP{String})\COLON{}T}, the
108	variable declaration
109	\EXP{x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = \VAR{stop}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{no}''})} instantiates
110	\VAR{stop} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the same call with no expected type
111	instantiates it at \TYP{Any}.
112	\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 did not
113	describe such a type parameter and left open whether inference may give it
114	\TYP{BottomType}, which the team's draft note at the end of this chapter asks.
115	The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that the rule by which the dispatcher of
116	the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments
117	do not fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, which never instantiates a
118	type parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, is the rule of static inference as well.}
119	\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
120	of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
121	is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
122	(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
123	parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
124	\end{itemize}
125	The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
126	as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.
127	
128	\emph{The expected type.}
129	A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
130	variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
131	right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
132	type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
133	as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, whether or not
134	local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
135	branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
136	expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
137	\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
138	every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
139	\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause
140	among them, the expected type of the \KWD{typecase} expression, of which the
141	union of the types of its clauses, the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression
142	(\secref{typecase}), is then a subtype where the type of each clause is; and
143	as the body of a \KWD{label} expression that has an expected type, or as the
144	\KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that
145	\KWD{label} expression, the expected type of the \KWD{label} expression, of
146	which the union of the type of its body and the types of those \KWD{with}
147	clause values, the type of the \KWD{label} expression (\secref{label-expr}),
148	is then a subtype where each of those types is.
149	The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
150	as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or by loose juxtaposition, as
151	\EXP{f\;x}, or as a method invocation or an operator application.
152	\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
153	gave the last expression of a block an expected type only where no local
154	declaration precedes it, and gave none to a clause of an \KWD{if} expression
155	without an \KWD{else} clause, to a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression or to
156	a call written by loose juxtaposition; the revival decided on 8~October 2026
157	that each has the type that the text already requires of it.
158	Its text of 8~October 2026 gave none to the body of a \KWD{label} expression
159	or to the \KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression; the
160	revival decided on 9~October 2026 that they have the expected type of the
161	\KWD{label} expression, as a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression has that of
162	the \KWD{typecase} expression.}
163	The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
164	the expected type.
165	If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
166	the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
167	then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
168	second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
169	(\secref{coercion}).
170	So, for the declarations
171	\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
172	and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
173	the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
174	instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
175	and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
176	instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
177	the result.
178	
179	\emph{Dispatch.}
180	The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
181	as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
182	coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.
183	
184	For example, of the declarations
185	\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
186	and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
187	\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has
188	type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, chooses the first, which is applicable without
189	coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
190	second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
191	and the converted call runs that instance.
192	\revision{revival-inference}{The interpreter has no static types and applies
193	the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments: it infers
194	the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
195	and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
196	type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
197	So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
198	or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a

5	\subsection{The contexts that give a call an expected type}
6	\seclabel{revival-expected-contexts}
7	
8	\begin{description}
9	\item[Affected sections] \secref{static-arg-inference}; \secref{numeral-default}.
10	\item[Change] The list of the contexts in which a call has an expected type,
11	in \secref{static-arg-inference}, gives the last expression of a block the
12	block's expected type whether or not local declarations precede it, and gains
13	two contexts: a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause,
14	whose expected type is \TYP{()}, and a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression
15	that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause among them, whose expected
16	type is that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
17	The sentence after the list says that the expected type is used also for a call
18	written by loose juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x}.
19	A second revision adds a third context to the list: the body of a \KWD{label}
20	expression that has an expected type, and the \KWD{with} clause expression of
21	each \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that \KWD{label} expression, whose
22	expected type is that of the \KWD{label} expression.
23	The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe, in
24	\secref{numeral-default}, names an argument of another call and the body of a
25	\KWD{for} loop, and no longer names the contexts that the list of contexts now
26	gives, the body of a \KWD{label} expression among them.
27	Each changed passage has a box.
28	How a call is instantiated under its expected type is unchanged.
29	\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
30	revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that these four contexts give a call the
31	type that the text already requires of them, a clause of a \KWD{typecase}
32	expression by the rule for the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
33	The text gives each context its type.
34	``If there is no \KWD{else} clause in an \KWD{if} expression, then every clause
35	must have type \EXP{()}'' (\secref{if-expr}).
36	``If the last element of the expression block is an expression, the value and
37	type of this expression are the value and type of the expression block as a
38	whole'' (\secref{block-expr}), whatever local declarations precede it.
39	The static arguments of an identifier reference ``are statically inferred from
40	the context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}), however the call is
41	written.
42	``The type of a \KWD{typecase} expression is the union of types of all
43	right-hand sides of the typecase clauses'' (\secref{typecase}), which is a
44	subtype of the expected type when the type of each clause is.
45	Since the revival's decision of 29~September 2026 a type parameter that nothing
46	at a call fixes takes the intersection of its upper bounds, never
47	\TYP{BottomType} (\secref{revival-inference}), so a call of \VAR{fail} or
48	\VAR{builtinPrimitive} of \library, whose type parameter only the result
49	mentions, took the bound \TYP{Any} in these contexts, and the compiled type
50	checker refused thirteen such calls of \library\ that the interpreter runs
51	(row~560 of the revival's gap ledger).
52	The alternative not taken was that the library write the static argument at
53	each such call, as \EXP{\VAR{fail}\llbracket()\rrbracket(s)}: the revival
54	decided that the library's own practice is the standard, and the library does
55	not route round a gap of the type checker.
56	A reversal would take the four contexts out of the list of contexts and back
57	into the item, and the compiled type checker would refuse those calls again.
58	The second revision follows the revival's decision of 9~October 2026 that the
59	body of a \KWD{label} expression and the \KWD{with} clause values of its exits
60	take the expected type of the whole \KWD{label} expression, as the clauses of a
61	\KWD{typecase} expression take that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
62	``The type of a \KWD{label} expression is the union of the type of the last
63	expression of its expression block and the types of the \KWD{with} clause
64	values of any \KWD{exit} expressions within the \KWD{label} expression whose
65	target is the \KWD{label} expression's name'' (\secref{label-expr}), which is a
66	subtype of the expected type when each of those types is.
67	The thirteenth of the calls of \library\ above ends a clause of a
68	\KWD{typecase} expression that ends the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and
69	took the bound \TYP{Any} there (row~642 of the revival's gap ledger).
70	A reversal of the second revision would take the body of a \KWD{label}
71	expression and its exits' \KWD{with} clause values out of the list of contexts
72	and back into the item, and the compiled type checker would refuse that call
73	again.

76	and, for the second revision, in
77	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md}
78	in the revival's repository.
79	\item[Effect] The compiled type checker gives these contexts their expected
80	types: it checks a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else}
81	clause against \TYP{()}, and it gives the expected type of the enclosing
82	expression to the last expression of a block after local declarations, to a
83	clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression, to the body of a \KWD{label} expression

(* A call written by loose juxtaposition is given the expected type of its value, which fixes a static argument that its argument or only its result mentions. *)
component InferLooseJuxtContext
export Executable

object BoxV[\T\](v: T) end
wrapV[\T\](x: T): BoxV[\T\] = BoxV[\T\](x)
stop[\T extends Any\](s: String): T = throw InvalidRange
giveUp(s: String): ZZ32 = stop s
gaveUp(): String = try "value " || giveUp("x") catch e InvalidRange => "thrown" end

run(): () = do
    e: BoxV[\ZZ64\] = wrapV 3
    assert(e.v = 3, "wrapV 3 with the expected type BoxV[ZZ64] is wrapV at ZZ64, the numeral converted; Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex, section \"Identifier References\"")
    assert(gaveUp(), "thrown", "stop s as the body of giveUp, whose return type is ZZ32, is instantiated at ZZ32 and throws; Specification/basic/inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
tests=InferLooseJuxtContext
compile
link
run
run_out_contains=PASS
tests=InferRepeatedOperatorContext
compile

run

(* An operator repeated between three operands has the expected type of its value, whether a multifix declaration accepts it or it is left-associated, so that type fixes a static argument that only the result mentions. *)
component InferRepeatedOperatorContext
export Executable

object BoxV[\T\]() end
tag(b: BoxV[\ZZ64\]): String = "ZZ64"
tag(b: BoxV[\String\]): String = "String"
opr OPLUS[\T\](a: Any, b: ZZ32): BoxV[\T\] = BoxV[\T\]()
opr OTIMES[\T\](a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32, c: ZZ32): BoxV[\T\] = BoxV[\T\]()

run(): () = do
    y: BoxV[\ZZ64\] = 1 OPLUS 2 OPLUS 3
    assert(tag(y), "ZZ64", "1 OPLUS 2 OPLUS 3, which no multifix declaration accepts, is (1 OPLUS 2) OPLUS 3, whose outer application the expected type BoxV[ZZ64] instantiates at ZZ64; Specification/basic/operators/chained-multifix.tex, section \"Chained and Multifix Operators\"; Specification/basic/inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\"")
    z: BoxV[\String\] = 1 OTIMES 2 OTIMES 3
    assert(tag(z), "String", "1 OTIMES 2 OTIMES 3 is the multifix application, which the expected type BoxV[String] instantiates at String; Specification/basic/operators/chained-multifix.tex, section \"Chained and Multifix Operators\"; Specification/basic/inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
component GenericBesidePlainTwoBounds
export Executable

(* A generic declaration whose type parameter has two bounds, beside two plain declarations one of which covers their overlap, is a valid overloading, and each call runs the most specific declaration. *)

trait Aa end
trait Bb end
object Both extends { Aa, Bb } end
object Both2 extends { Aa, Bb } end

w[\T extends { Aa, Bb }\](x: T, y: ZZ32): String = "generic"
w(x: Both, y: Any): String = "bothAny"
w(x: Both, y: ZZ32): String = "meet"

run(): () = do
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    assert(w(Both, z), "meet", "a Both with a ZZ32 takes the declaration on Both and ZZ32, below the other two; the generic declaration and the one on Both and Any overlap only where Both and ZZ32 meet, and that declaration covers it; Specification/advanced/overloading.tex, section \"Declarations with Static Parameters\"")
    assert(w(Both2, z), "generic", "another object below both bounds with a ZZ32 takes the generic declaration")
    assert(w(Both, "s"), "bothAny", "a Both with a String takes the declaration on Both and Any")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

shown(v: Any): String = v.asString || " : " || v.ilkName

run(): () = do
    u = vector[\ZZ32,3\]()
    u[0] := 1
    u[1] := 2
    u[2] := 3
    w = vector[\ZZ32,3\]()
    w[0] := 4
    w[1] := 5
    w[2] := 6
    assert(shown(u.dot(w)), "32 : Int", "an integer vector's dot product stays an integer; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Vector, dot")
    assert(shown(u.scale(2)[2]), "6 : Int", "an integer vector scaled by an integer; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Vector, scale")
    assert(shown((u + w)[1]), "7 : Int", "an integer vector sum; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Vector, opr +")

    rv = vector[\RR64,2\]()
    rv[0] := 0.5
    rv[1] := 1.5
    assert(rv.dot(rv), 2.5, "a float vector's dot product; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Vector, dot")
    assert(rv.scale(2.0)[1], 3.0, "a float vector scaled by a float; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Vector, scale")

    k = matrix[\ZZ32,2,2\]()
    k[0,0] := 1
    k[0,1] := 2
    k[1,0] := 3
    k[1,1] := 4
    kk = k k
    assert(shown(kk[0,0]), "7 : Int", "an integer matrix product; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Matrix, mul")
    assert(kk[0,1], 10, "an integer matrix product; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Matrix, mul")
    assert(kk[1,0], 15, "an integer matrix product; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Matrix, mul")
    assert(kk[1,1], 22, "an integer matrix product; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, trait Matrix, mul")

    iv = array[\ZZ32\](3).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => i - 1)
    assert(shown((iv MIN 0)[2]), "0 : Int", "an integer array's MIN with an integer; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr MIN on an array and a number")
    assert(shown((0 MAX iv)[0]), "0 : Int", "an integer's MAX with an integer array; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr MAX on a number and an array")
    assert(shown((iv + 1)[0]), "0 : Int", "an integer array plus an integer; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr + on an array and a number")
    assert(shown((1 - iv)[0]), "2 : Int", "an integer minus an integer array; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr - on a number and an array")
    fv = array[\RR64\](3).tabulate(fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 1.0 i - 1.0)
    assert((fv MAX 0.5)[0], 0.5, "a float array's MAX with a float; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr MAX on an array and a number")
    assert((0.5 MIN fv)[2], 0.5, "a float's MIN with a float array; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, opr MIN on a number and an array")

    rm = matrix[\RR64,2,2\](2.0)
    assert(rm[0,0], 2.0, "matrix(v) puts v on the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
    assert(rm[0,1], 0.0, "matrix(v) puts zero off the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
    three: NN32 = unsigned(3)
    nm = matrix[\NN32,2,2\](three)
    assert(shown(nm[1,1]), "3 : NN32", "matrix(v) of an NN32 puts v on the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
    assert(shown(nm[0,1]), "0 : NN32", "matrix(v) of an NN32 puts the NN32 zero off the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
    four: NN64 = unsigned(4)
    lm = matrix[\NN64,2,2\](four)
    assert(shown(lm[1,0]), shown(four.zero), "matrix(v) of an NN64 puts the NN64 zero off the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
    assert(lm[0,0], four, "matrix(v) of an NN64 puts v on the diagonal; Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, matrix")
  end

end

== explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:365-375

## B.7 Overloading

Resolution is split between a shared rewrite and two completely different dispatch mechanisms.

The shared part: `OverloadRewriter` replaces a reference that has several candidates with a reference to a single synthetic name spelled `f{f1,f2,…}` and appends a `_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` declaring it (`compiler/OverloadRewriter.java:74-92`, `OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:110-142`).

On the interpreter path, `BuildTopLevelEnvironments.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildTopLevelEnvironments.java:128`) turns that declaration into an `OverloadedFunction`, and the actual selection happens per call, on run-time values, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787`); failure is the familiar "Failed to find any matching overload" (`:795`).

On the compiler path, `CodeGen.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6409`) hands the declaration to `OverloadSet`, which emits one dispatch method per overloaded name, testing argument types from most to least specific (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1944,1964`).

So the same phase feeds a run-time search in one world and a generated decision tree in the other, and the candidate lists they start from are different (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`): the interpreter's comes from the disambiguator, the compiler's from the type checker.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,

explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:45:- **The static-parameter sentence goes (answer 9).** The specification's sentence that overloads may not differ in static parameters is dropped; the specification is revised to the type group's 2011 model the checker runs, the original kept as superseded text in the S1 form. The checker keeps the paper's three rules with two changes: the return-type rule is checked over every instance, and one narrow rule stays, that two generic arms in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters position by position (Java's overriding rule; it closes row 398). Walk dispatches by declared domains, which ends its dependence on declaration order. The library's refused families are repaired by its own devices. No model line changes. The judgement's section 10 items (walk and an unused unknown size, `seq`'s device, Naden's instantiation) took the record's defaults, listed for his review, and what the build left open for him is listed in `PLAN.md` beside them.
explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:46:- **Conversions never change which declaration runs.** A conversion is applied to make a call possible and never changes which declaration runs when one already fits; declarations are chosen by the coercion chapter's order, applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them (a generic declaration fits when some instance within its bound fits); the chosen declaration is then instantiated by answer 8's promotion, its coercions inserted statically, and the rewritten call dispatches on the converted values; a numeral whose candidate types are incomparable reads as `ZZ32` (`ZZ64` or `ZZ` by magnitude), stated once in the inference chapter. So a generic arm over `T extends Number` beside a plain arm over `Any` runs the generic at `ZZ64` for a mixed-width call, the specialised instance; plain declarations are untouched; the broader rule (his own idea, "if there is a conversion to a specific type, it should be applied. And only if all combinations are exhausted and we haven't reached a specific implementation, then we go to a plain implementation") is not taken. His principle behind it: "we must make it fast, and generic is never fast. So make it fast." — fast code a JVM can specialise. With it, the inference rule: the checker infers a static argument with coercion, answer 8's promotion its number case, and keeps the expected type at a call written `f(x)` with a retry without it, so that a binding's coercion still applies; walk does the same at dispatch, re-instantiating the chosen declaration by the promotion from run-time types; the specification's type-inference chapter states it in the S1 form. Built: the checker and walk infer as stated, walk dispatching a converted call again (FACTS, "Walk chooses between a generic declaration and another on their declared domains ..."); the numeral tie rule is stated once, in the inference chapter; the stock compiled crash is a row closed by a test (row 504); the two-generic dispatcher defect is gated for phase 5 (row 537).
explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:50:- **A `label` body takes the expected type of the whole `label` (item 48, row 642).** The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and its exits' `with` values (`Specification/basic/expressions/label.tex:66-70`), so, as for a `typecase` clause (batch 11's Q2, way 1), the checker passes the expected type of the whole into the body and the exits' values; the inference chapter's list of contexts gains them and Appendix I's entry is amended in the S1 form. A call written as the argument of another call (row 455) is measured by a probe before it is put to him again; his reading is that this unifies the inference rules everywhere, covering cases the team did not build, and that where the mechanism is known it goes ahead. He took (a) after the explanation that `label` is a named block left early by `exit` with a value, not a goto, and that a block's value is its last expression, as in Scala and Swift.
explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:53:- **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ` and raise at +∞, −∞ and 0/0 (item 44, row 635).** The declared integer result and the peers win over the specification's paragraph that these methods return the argument at an infinity (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:456-472`), which is revised in the S1 form; the library's bodies (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:646`, `:651`) raise instead of returning `self`, and the pin at `ProjectFortress/tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss:23` changes, its before and after listed for him. explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:54:- **Arithmetic in a size: the checker compares size expressions by their written form after folding numerals, and a size name may equal a numeral (item 15, 15a with (b)).** The checker accepts a sum, difference, product or power in a size, compares two size expressions by their form once numerals are folded (`2 3` is `6`; `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`), and range-checks what it folds; the class loader computes the value when it makes a class; a size name counts as possibly equal to a numeral, as the team's Q&A answers (`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex:167-198`), so the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:94:- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. A tight juxtaposition without any dots might not be entirely left-associated.
Rather, it is considered as a nonempty sequence of elements: the front
expression, any ``math items'', and any postfix operator, and subject to
reassociation as described below.  A math item may be a subscripting,
an exponentiation, or one of a few kinds of expressions.
It is a static error if an exponentiation is immediately followed by
a subcripting or an exponentiation.

The procedure for reassociation is as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item For each expression element (i.e., not a subscripting, exponentiation or
postfix operator), determine whether it is a function.
\item If some function element is immediately followed by an expression element
then, find the first such function element, and call the next element the
argument.  It is a static error if either the argument is not parenthesized,
or the argument is immediately followed by a non-expression element.  Otherwise,
replace the function and argument with a single element that is the application
of the function to the argument.  This new element is an expression.
Reassociate the resulting sequence (which is one element shorter).
\item If there is any non-expression element (it cannot be the first element)
then replace the first such element and the element immediately preceding it
(which must be an expression) with a single element that does the appropriate
operator application.  This new element is an expression.  Reassociate the
resulting sequence (which is one element shorter).
\item Otherwise, the sequence necessarily has only expression elements,
only the last of which may be a function.
If any element that remains has type String, then it is a static error
if there is any pair of adjacent elements within the juxtaposition
such that neither element is of type String.

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

problem: rung E's skeptic's measurements of row 644 and of row 651's second shape (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/SKEPTIC.md:87-95`, `:62-85`), with the expected failures `XXXInferRepeatedOperatorContext`, `XXXMethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOther` and `XXXMethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOtherSameName` at the base, and the distance stage's per-site list, 'Function body has type Any, but declared return type is ().' at `Library/String.fss:431` (row 642), in the batch record's rung C (`explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv:117`; `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-12.md:208`)

## 1. What changed, and why

Under the curator's answer to Q48's part (a) (POSITIONS, "A `label` body takes the expected type of the whole `label` (item 48, row 642)."), and for rows 644 and 651 whatever that answer, the compiled checker now:

- **Row 644.** Gives an operator repeated between three or more operands the expected type of its value (`impls/Operators.scala:379-393`). Whether the multifix application applies is still decided without the expected type. Where it applies, it is checked again with the expected type, and that check is kept if it succeeds. Otherwise the left-associated binary applications are checked with the expected type, so the outer application has it. This is the loose juxtaposition's form since rung E (`:170-197`). The chapter's sentence after the list already gave an operator application the expected type (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:149-151`). The multifix rule is `chained-multifix.tex:42-48`.
- **Row 642 (under Q48).** Checks the body of a `label` with the label's expected type (`impls/Misc.scala:707-710`), and the `with` value of each `exit` to it with the same type (`:733-739`). `labelExitTypes` is the map that the checkers of one compilation unit share. The label's entry in it is now a `LabelExitTypes` (`:991-996`), a set of exit types that also keeps the label's expected type, and the exit reads the type from there. The label's type stays the join of the body's and the exits' types (`:717`), so it is a subtype of the expected type wherever each of them is. This is the union rule that the curator read for a `typecase` clause (batch 11's Q2) and for the label (Q48).
- **Row 651.** Checks a written static argument of a dotted method against its parameter's bounds with the written arguments put in (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:771-800`). A `StaticTypeReplacer` of the method's own parameters by the written arguments replaces in each `extends` and `dominates` bound before the subtype check. An argument that does not meet its substituted bound is now refused as any inapplicable method is: 'No such method O.gen.' (section 6).

import os, re, sys, collections

}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

diff --git a/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala b/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala
index 31472e0fe..edb73b3c0 100644
--- a/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala
+++ b/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala
@@ -469,28 +469,24 @@ class TypeSchemaAnalyzer(implicit val ta: TypeAnalyzer) {
     }
 //    println("  imageSparams = " + imageSparams)
     
-    // Create a type analyzer with only the image variables and their bounds.
-    val imageTa = ta.extend(imageSparams, None)
-    // The bounds are the conjuncts of their meet where each conjunct is a
-    // BaseType. The meet of bounds one of which is a trait with a comprises
-    // clause can be a union, which a bound list cannot hold; the bounds are
-    // then kept as the list they are, each already a BaseType.
+    // The bounds are kept as the list they are, each already a BaseType, without
+    // Any and duplicates, and never met into one type: the meet of bounds one of
+    // which is a trait with a comprises clause can be a union, which a bound
+    // list cannot hold, and normalizing it expands that trait into its members.
     val rimageSparams = imageSparams.map{
       case SStaticParam(i, v, x, e, doms, d, a, k:KindType, l) =>
-        val met = conjuncts(imageTa.meet(e)).toList
-        val bds = if (met.forall(_.isInstanceOf[BaseType])) met.map(_.asInstanceOf[BaseType])
-                  else removeDuplicates(e).map(_.asInstanceOf[BaseType])
+        val bds = removeDuplicates(e.filterNot(_.isInstanceOf[AnyType])).map(_.asInstanceOf[BaseType])
         SStaticParam(i, v, x, bds, doms, d, a, k, l)
       case x => x
     }
 //    println("  rimageSparams = " + rimageSparams)
     val rimageTa = ta.extend(rimageSparams, None)
     // Verify that the image environment can prove that each variable's image
-    // is a subtype of all its bounds' images.
+    // is a subtype of all its bounds' images, one bound at a time.
     // Sizes have no bounds; a nat or int parameter is kept as it is.
     val sizeSparams = sparams.filter(sp => sp.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindNat] || sp.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindInt])
     if (varsMap.forall { case (x, xbds) =>
-      rimageTa.lteq(phi(x), phi(imageTa.meet(xbds)))
+      xbds.forall(b => rimageTa.lteq(phi(x), phi(b)))
     }) Some(rimageSparams ++ sizeSparams) // Success -- return the image's static params.
     else None             // Failure
   }

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason
#   SETTING CHANGED         the two tables ran different settings: the counts are not like for like
#   SHADOW STALE            a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources
# A move of 2 to 4 errors in the components' type errors or in which pair of LEXICO, SQCAP or
# INVERSE declarations an overloading error names is the checker's run-to-run variation
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md section 5), not a change; a crash row whose line numbers
# moved because a rung edited above it prints as one gone and one new.
DistanceMulti.java

classify.py
compare.sh
errors.py
run.sh

# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" \
      "$D/WorldFlip.java" "$D/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
      > "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" 2>&1
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then
    echo "checker-count: javac failed; see $SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; tail -20 "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 2. run the compiler phase order over the interpreter's library under a private cache
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 10 900 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" \
       -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=$OVERLOAD_CACHE \
       -cp "$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" WorldFlip "$TARGET" ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
RC=$?
if ! grep -q 'has [0-9]* errors\?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ; then
    echo "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=$RC); see $SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2
    tail -20 "$SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 3. the table. One row per api the checker named, its own error count as the
#    instrumented checker printed it; then the total, the number of distinct
#    file:line the errors were reported at, and the first crash the checker
#    survived. Rows are sorted so that two runs of the same tree are byte-equal.
{
    printf '#api\terrors\n'
    grep '^@@PROBE checkApi .* -> errors=' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
        | sed -E 's/^@@PROBE checkApi ([^ ]+) -> errors=([0-9]+)$/\1\t\2/' | sort -u
    printf '#total\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE 'has [0-9]+ errors?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | tail -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+')"
    printf '#locations\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE '^/[^ ]+:[0-9]+:' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
    crash=$(grep -m1 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sed 's/^@@PROBE //')
    site=$(grep -m1 -A6 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
           | grep -oE '\([A-Za-z0-9_$]+\.(scala|java):[0-9]+\)' | grep -v '(NI\.java:' \
           | head -1 | tr -d '()')      # the first frame that is not the nyi helper itself
    printf '#crash\t%s\n' "${crash:-none}${site:+ at $site}"
    printf '#cache\toverloading memo %s (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=%s)\n' \
           "$( [ "$OVERLOAD_CACHE" = false ] && echo off || echo on )" "$OVERLOAD_CACHE"
    if [ "$(sha256sum < "$STOCK" | cut -d' ' -f1)" = "$STOCK_SHA" ] ; then
        printf '#shadow\tmatches the tracked StaticChecker\n'
    else
        printf '#shadow\tSTALE: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java has changed since the copy was taken; refresh the copy and the checksum in run.sh\n'
    fi
} > "$OUT"

content.content:
## 9. Found on the way

- **The model's numeral powers are refused by the compiled checker since climb batch N's rung I.** `10.0^(-5)`, `10.0^(-8)`, `-(10.0^10)` and the check program's three tolerances meet `RR64`'s `^` on an `RR64` and `MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\]`'s `^` on a `ZZ64`, both only by converting the integer; the tie is refused, and the refusal ends the check of its block (`rebase-2026-09-29/measure/base.own.txt`, `d.own.txt`, `d-split-e3.own.txt`). Walk takes them. No ledger row names it; the declarations are `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:278` and `:358`.
- **The comment that decision D's note of 2026-09-27 called the library's own is the revival's.** "sized arrays under a compiler need per-shape declarations beside these" was written by the revival on 2026-09-23 (`c2b4e2c95`) and reworded on 2026-09-28 (`581356f32`); today it reads "a static checker sees only Array[\T,I\], so the rank and size of a sized argument are lost to it in the result" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2595-2600`). The team's own statement on per-type storage is Maessen's commit message of 2008 (section 3).
- **A two-trait bound on the array traits makes the compiled checker's Meet Rule check of the library several times slower.** With `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` on `Vector` and `Matrix`, `FortressLibrary` took 3,825 s against 704 s unchanged, most of it in the component's overloading stage, in nested exclusion tests through the `comprises` check (section 7; `captures/distance-RINGNUM-stack.txt`). Not a pair of one run; batch 8's Meet Rule work (class M1, 109 errors) runs in the same code.
- **Decision E's patch applies again.** `rebase-2026-09-29/library-e3.patch` is the 17 dead sizes regenerated on today's library; `git apply --check` passes.

## 10. What is measured, what is read, what was not run

- **Measured here:** the re-based diff on seven checker copies and under walk (section 2); the four decision A probes on both paths (section 3); four library copies and an unchanged one through the distance stage, the team's array tests under walk against five copies, and C4's check program against one (sections 4 and 7); D3's `T^n` on both paths (section 2); the two width pairs (section 6).
- **Cited from the record, not re-run:** the batch N gate's distance table and sites, today's tree (V1, V2, Z1); the boxing costs of `perf-probes/kernels/` and `reviews/array-design-review.md`; the design B size machinery (FACTS lines 42, 43, 114); the peers' survey of `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 6 and `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` § g.

content.content:
\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}

that an ordinary type can appear, except that a naked type variable must not
appear in the \KWD{extends} clause of a trait or object declaration,

usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

With the array family bounded by T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\\T\\] }
and the crash fixed, the checker-count stage's api check of FortressLibrary
took about 18 minutes (17:47:05 to 18:05:06 UTC), past the stage's 900 s
limit, where the base takes seconds: every subtype query on such a variable
expands Number's comprises clause in TypeAnalyzer (rung N's file). So the
library's bounds, the scalar block's and matrix(v)'s v.zero are taken back
to the base's text, and ArrayElementAlgebra keeps only what the base runs.

are, without Any and duplicates, and checks a variable against each bound in
turn, with no proof for a bound the variable was itself given; no meet of a
bound list is formed. Appendix I's entry 'The contexts that give a call an
expected type' says the checker gives a tight juxtaposition its expected type
(row 660). Edits the original tree: TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala, changes.tex.

84:- **The compiled checker instantiates a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes at the intersection of its upper bounds, never `BottomType`, and tries a call by subtyping without the expected type first** (`compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md`). `Formula.solveToBounds` (`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:489-583`) solves a call's static arguments: no named lower bound, the meet of the upper bounds (declared bound, expected type), each taken at the solutions of the other variables it mentions where those are found, a bound that still mentions a variable, the variable itself among them, left out (row 593); an empty meet, no solution; unconstrained, `Any`. A lone parameter's union is promoted to its bound; an intersection argument is a whole lower bound (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:137-138`). Attempts: subtyping without the context, kept when its result converts; subtyping, then coercion, with it; coercion without (`Functionals.scala:703-716`). The compiled run time does not load an instance at an intersection, which the rule gives by two routes (row 559). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferResultOnly*`, `InferLoneUnbounded`, `InferUnion*Arg`, `InferLoneBoundThree`, `CoverageReturnInferred`, `XXXInferLoneUnionClosedTrait`, `InferContextKeepsFit`, `ExpectedType*Choice`, `InferBigOperatorUnwritten`, `InferResultOnlyIfWithoutElse`, `InferBoundMeetsExpectedTrait`. The one library's result-only `fail` and `builtinPrimitive`, unbounded, are refused where no expected type reaches the call, which is only at an argument of another call (row 455), since a `label` body takes the expected type of the whole `label` (row 642, `Library/String.fss:431`; "The compiled checker gives a call its expected type ..." below); where `()` is expected their instance is `()` ("The one library's numbers, orderings, List and natives answer their declared types ..." below).
91:- **The one library's generator, condition, reduction and generator-of-generators slips are repaired in the library's own spelling; the sites left there are a `Generator`'s size and index, the identities' numeral fallback, `embiggen` and `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm** (`compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md`; rows 627 to 633). Condition's `cond` calls take their result type as static argument, as Maybe's `map` does; `__whileCond` answers `Boolean`; the eight big operators with no declared return type take the api's; Generator2's `theorems` answer `ZeroIndexed`, `FilterGenerator2` narrows `g` to `Generator2`, `relationalPredicate` answers a function of a `Generator`. Six repaired declarations that stopped walk now answer the value their bodies state, and an ill-typed `MIMapReduceReduction` whose identity is not an `R` is refused where walk printed it. Left: `|g|`, `g.size` and `g[i]` on a `Generator` (629), the identities' numeral fallback (630), `embiggen` (631) and `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm (632); the sites of walk's `Any` devices in the reductions (row 628) and of the capture (row 627) are gone ("The identity-less reductions are typed at their element type ..." under "Landed semantics"; "The compiled checker gives a call its expected type ..." below). Gated by `tests/GeneratorDeclarations.fss`.
93:- **The compiled checker gives a call its expected type in a clause of an `if` without `else` (`()`), a block's last expression after local declarations, a `typecase` clause and a loose juxtaposition, and renames an inherited method's own static parameters apart from the receiver's static arguments** (`compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md`, `compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md`; rows 560, 627, 642, 644 and 651 fixed). It also gives one to an operator repeated between three or more operands and to the body of a `label` and its exits' `with` values, and it checks a written static argument of a method against its bounds with the written arguments put in. The sites in `impls/Misc.scala`: `:583-584` (the `if` without `else`); `:326`, `:340` and `:662-667` (the `typecase`); `:704-739` (the `label`). The label's body gets the type directly. Each exit's `with` value gets it through the label's entry in `labelExitTypes`, a `LabelExitTypes` that keeps the expected type (`:996`). The other sites: `impls/Decls.scala:51-58` (`checkLetBody`), `impls/Operators.scala:170-197` (the loose juxtaposition) and `:382-393` (the repeated operator). In both of the last two, whether the multifix application applies is decided without the expected type. The type is then given to the multifix application where it fits, and otherwise to the left-associated binary fallback. `STypesUtil.instantiateMethodApart` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1822-1863`) instantiates each method that `commonInheritedMethods` returns. It first renames to `name$i` each of the method's own static parameters whose name the arguments mention, so the method invocation and a call by name inside a trait are repaired alike. `staticArgsMatchStaticParamsForApp` (`STypesUtil.scala:771-800`) puts the written arguments into each bound with a `StaticTypeReplacer`, as `TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:157-162` does for a trait type's arguments. An argument that misses its bound is refused: 'No such method O.gen.' The checker still gives no expected type to an argument of another call (row 455, `XXXInferContextDrops`), or to the application of the juxtaposition operator that a tight juxtaposition of items none of which is a function stands for, as `a(b)` (row 660, `XXXInferTightJuxtContext`): `impls/Operators.scala:362-374` tries the multifix and the binary applications there with none. The checker of an `atomic` or `tryatomic` body (`AtomicChecker`, `impls/Misc.scala:960-989`) refuses a `spawn` wherever it checks one, with an expected type or without (`:983-988`), so a `spawn` that is an exit's `with` value is refused as before the label's repair, and one that ends an atomic block, where the checker had stopped, 'Not in the trait table: CompilerBuiltin.Thread', is refused too; gated by `XXXSpawnInAtomicExitValue` beside the team's `XXX1am`, `XXX1ap` and `XXX9i`. Gated by `compiler_tests/InferResultOnlyIfWithoutElse`, `InferResultOnlyAfterLocalDecl`, `InferResultOnlyTypecaseBranch`, `InferLooseJuxtContext`, `InferRepeatedOperatorContext`, `InferResultOnlyLabelBody` (a `typecheck` test, since the code generator has no `label`), `MethodStaticArgReceiverSameName`, `MethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOther`, `MethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOtherSameName` and `InheritedMethodByNameStaticParamSameName`, and by `XXXLooseJuxtMultifixExpectedType`, a refusal.
- **The compiled checker gives a call its expected type in a clause of an `if` without `else` (`()`), a block's last expression after local declarations, a `typecase` clause and a loose juxtaposition, and renames an inherited method's own static parameters apart from the receiver's static arguments** (`compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md`, `compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md`; rows 560, 627, 642, 644 and 651 fixed). It also gives one to an operator repeated between three or more operands and to the body of a `label` and its exits' `with` values, and it checks a writ
154:- **Route A's generic container obligations still need body-level checks** (`reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review.md`; measured by the flattening, `compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md` sections 12 and 13). `Vector` and `Matrix` promise scalar results of `T`; on the flat library their operations and the scalar-extension block run under `walk` for all seven number types (the norm with an explicit `asFloat`), except `matrix(v)` for `NN32` and `NN64` (row 437), while the checker refuses the generic bodies' arithmetic at `(T, T)`: a body bounded only by `T extends Number` has no evidence for its arithmetic. Still to test: row 388's `m.scale(i)` against the generic operator `m i`, and empty reductions' advertised result type as well as their identity.
